item.text: {"text":"The closest GRU-specific precedent is [MTAM (CIKM 2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598): learned temporal gates modify recurrent state transitions and attention, combining time-aware GRU short-term intent with historical memory. Within 2023–2026, relevant findings include [TLSTSRec (online 2024)](https://doi.org/10.3233/IDA-240051), which models temporal information and long/short-term preferences, and [Long-Term Interest Clock (WWW 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15817), which retrieves historical behaviors and aggregates them using time-gap-aware attention. These support adaptive temporal modeling as a hypothesis, but do not establish that a decay-gated GRU improves this Amazon benchmark.\n\n[RepeatNet (AAAI 2019)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/4408) explicitly models repeat versus exploratory consumption. Its direct repeat-item mechanism is less applicable to unseen-item recommendations; repeated historical interactions could instead inform retention within one jointly trained GRU. Practical inference from these papers: condition GRU retention on elapsed-time features and observed recurrence, then compare against the corrected baseline using macro validation HR@10. First verify padding invariance: padding must leave recurrent state unchanged, and readout must select the final nonpadding position. Interpret learned retention as predictive association; timestamps and repetition alone do not establish purchase readiness or durable preference."}
